title: System Log 1: Defining a protocol
lessonSummary: Great! You wrote your first system protocol and ran it several times.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: One protocol is defined once and called twice.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def start_scan():
    print("Scan started...")
    print("Checking sector!")

start_scan()
start_scan()

tasks.instruction: Define a function charge_energy() that prints exactly Energy charged! and call it three times.

validation.expected:
Energy charged!
Energy charged!
Energy charged!

tasks.instruction: Define a function open_hatch() that prints exactly Hatch open. Call it once, then print exactly Done! (outside the function).

title: System Log 2: One parameter
lessonSummary: Nice! Your protocol can now work with different inputs.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: The same protocol reports two different crew members.
Write a function scan_planet(planet) that prints Scanning: <planet> Call it with "Mars" and then with "Titan".
Write a function show_energy(energy) that prints Energy: <energy> % Call it with the numbers 80 and 35 (without quotes).

title: System Log 3: Several parameters
lessonSummary: Great! Your protocols now take several inputs in the right order.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: Three arguments fill three parameters – in the right order.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def register_crew(name, role, level):
    print(f"Name: {name}")
    print(f"Role: {role}")
    print(f"Level: {level}")

register_crew("Nova", "Pilot", 5)

tasks.instruction: Write a function fire(weapon, power) that prints Shot with <weapon>: <power> energy Call it with ("Laser", 40) and then with ("Plasma", 75).

validation.expected:
Shot with Laser: 40 energy
Shot with Plasma: 75 energy

tasks.instruction: The function send_message(recipient, text) is already finished. Call it so that it prints exactly To Nova: Course correct Watch the order of the arguments!

title: System Log 4: Returning values with return
lessonSummary: Nice! Your protocols now deliver results you can keep calculating with.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: The result is stored and used right away.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def calculate_usage(modules, output):
    return modules * output

usage = calculate_usage(3, 20)
print(f"Usage: {usage} kW")
print(f"Full load: {calculate_usage(10, 50)} kW")

tasks.instruction: Write a function double_shield(level) that returns level * 2 with return. Print exactly Shield doubled: 14 by using double_shield(7).
Write a function calculate_credits(jobs, per_job) that returns jobs * per_job. Store calculate_credits(5, 40) in the variable credits and print exactly Cyber Credits: 200

title: System Log 5: return or print?
lessonSummary: Well spotted! You now know when a protocol prints and when it returns.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: A function without return gives back None.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def show_status():
    print("All systems running.")

result = show_status()
print(f"Return value: {result}")

tasks.instruction: The function calculate_supplies calculates the need but does not return it – that is why it prints Supplies: None. Add return so that exactly Supplies: 21 is printed.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def calculate_supplies(crew, days):
    total = crew * days

supplies = calculate_supplies(7, 3)
print(f"Supplies: {supplies}")

tasks.instruction: Write a function total_price(price, amount) that returns price * amount. Use it: total = total_price(30, 3), credits = 100 - total. Print exactly Credits left: 10

title: System Log 6: Decisions and loops in functions
lessonSummary: Masterful! Your protocols can now decide and repeat.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: The function returns a different text depending on the shield strength.
Write a function is_fast(speed) that returns True if speed is at least 100, otherwise False. Print is_fast(150) and then is_fast(60) with print.

Write a function count_signals(sectors) that adds all numbers from 1 to sectors with a for loop (sector 1 sends 1 signal, sector 2 sends two signals, …) and returns the sum. Print exactly Signals: 55 by using count_signals(10).

title: System Log 7: Docstrings and good names
lessonSummary: Excellent! Your protocols now have descriptions and good names.

tasks.instruction: Run this example: The docstring is shown with __doc__.
tasks.codeTemplate:
def calculate_fuel(distance):
    """Calculates the fuel requirement."""
    return distance * 3

print(calculate_fuel.__doc__)
print(calculate_fuel(10))

tasks.instruction: Write a function show_alarm() with the docstring "Shows the alarm status." (in triple quotes) that prints Alarm: All quiet. First print show_alarm.__doc__, then call the function.

validation.expected:
Shows the alarm status.
Alarm: All quiet.

tasks.instruction: The function is called cs(l, w) – a bad name. Rename it to calculate_cargo_space(length, width) (also the parameters in the body) so the call below works and prints exactly Cargo space: 21

title: Debug Quest
lessonSummary: All bugs found! With functions, indentation, the parentheses on the call and return matter.

tasks.instruction: 🐛 Bug #1 – Goal: The program should print Scan running! What is wrong?
🐛 Bug #2 – Goal: The program should print Energy: 10 (for 5 modules). What is wrong?
tasks.codeTemplate:
def calculate_energy(modules):
    return modules * 2

result = calculate_energy
print(f"Energy: {result}")

tasks.instruction: 🐛 Bug #3 – Goal: The program should print Credits: 8. What is wrong?
tasks.codeTemplate:
def add_credits(a, b):
    result = a + b

credits = add_credits(5, 3)
print(f"Credits: {credits}")

title: Mission 1: The Ship Technician Apprentice
lessonSummary: The Ship Technician Apprentice is trained: You wrote protocols, called them and delivered results!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Greeting: Write a function greet_crew() that prints exactly Welcome aboard! Call it twice.
Step 2 – Calculate energy: Write a function calculate_energy(modules, output) that returns modules * output. Print exactly Energy: 60 by using calculate_energy(5, 12).

Step 3 – Enough energy? Write a function is_energy_ok(demand, supply) that returns True if supply is at least demand, otherwise False. Print Drive: True (demand 30, supply 50) and then Weapons: False (demand 40, supply 25).

title: Mission 2: The Mission Planner
lessonSummary: The Mission Planner stands: Your functions now build complete mission reports!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Profit: Write a function calculate_profit(jobs, failures) that returns jobs * 10 - failures * 5. Print exactly Profit: 70 by using calculate_profit(8, 2).
Step 2 – ID: Write a function create_id(name, number) that returns the text <number>: <name> Print exactly 7: Nova by printing create_id("Nova", 7).

Step 3 – Mission report: The functions from steps 1 and 2 are provided. Write show_mission_report(name, number, jobs, failures) that prints three lines: the ID, Profit: <profit> and Failures: <failures> Call it with ("Nova", 7, 8, 2).

title: Mission 3: The Maintenance Calculator
lessonSummary: The Maintenance Calculator runs: Duration, energy check and display work hand in hand!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Duration: Write a function calculate_maintenance(hours) that returns hours * 5 (minutes). Print exactly Maintenance: 40 minutes by using calculate_maintenance(8).

Step 2 – Serviceable? Write a function is_serviceable(energy, duration) that returns True if energy is at least duration * 2, otherwise False. Print Nebula: True (energy 90, duration 40) and then Comet: False (energy 60, duration 40).

Step 3 – Maintenance display: The two functions are provided. Write show_maintenance(ship, energy, hours): It prints <ship>: maintenance <duration> minutes if the ship may be serviced, otherwise <ship>: needs recharge. Call it with ("Nebula", 90, 8) and ("Comet", 60, 8).

validation.expected:
Nebula: maintenance 40 minutes
Comet: needs recharge

title: Extra Challenge 1: The Shield System
lessonSummary: The Shield System runs: Bonus, shield strength and display fit together!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Shield bonus: Write a function calculate_shield_bonus(modules): From 5 modules there are 20 bonus points, from 3 modules 10, otherwise 0. For 6, 4 and 1 modules print Bonus: 20, Bonus: 10 and Bonus: 0 one after another.

Step 2 – Shield strength: calculate_shield_bonus is provided. Write calculate_shield(energy, modules) that returns energy * 3 + shield bonus. Print exactly Shield: 110 by using calculate_shield(30, 6).

Step 3 – Display: Both functions are provided. Write show_shield(name, energy, modules) that prints <name>: shield <strength>, and call it in a for loop for "Nova" with energy 30 and the module counts 2, 4 and 6 (range(2, 7, 2)).

validation.expected:
Nova: shield 90
Nova: shield 100
Nova: shield 110

title: Extra Challenge 2: The Fleet Manager
lessonSummary: The Fleet Manager stands: Demand, supply and report work together!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Fuel: Write a function calculate_fuel(ships, days) that returns ships * days * 4. Print exactly Fuel: 280 by using calculate_fuel(10, 7).

Step 2 – Is the supply enough? Write a function is_fuel_enough(demand, supply) that returns True if supply is at least demand, otherwise False. Print Enough: True (demand 280, supply 300) and then Enough: False (demand 280, supply 200).

Step 3 – Report: Both functions are provided. Write fleet_report(fleet, ships, days, supply) that prints three lines: Fleet <fleet>, Fuel: <demand> and Enough: <True/False>. Call it with ("Alpha", 10, 7, 300).

title: Extra Challenge 3: The Chase
lessonSummary: The Chase runs: Speed, legs and result fit together!

tasks.instruction: Step 1 – Speed: Write a function calculate_speed(base, ballast) that returns base - ballast, but never less than 0. Print Speed: 25 (base 40, ballast 15) and then Speed: 0 (base 10, ballast 30).

Step 2 – Leg: Write a function fly_leg(distance, speed) that returns the new remaining distance (distance - speed, but never below 0). Start with distance = 100, call fly_leg(distance, 25) twice (store the result in distance again) and print Distance: <distance> after each call.

Step 3 – Chase: fly_leg is provided. Write simulate_chase(distance, speed, legs): A for loop (leg 1 to legs) calls fly_leg each time and prints Leg <number>: <distance> km to go At the end the function returns the remaining distance. Call it with (100, 30, 4), store the result in left and print Left: <left>

validation.expected:
Leg 1: 70 km to go
Leg 2: 40 km to go
Leg 3: 10 km to go
Leg 4: 0 km to go
Left: 0
